about: TuxCopilot's command catalogue: every command the Commands section explains, finds and opens a page for. Plain words for someone who has just installed Arch. 'words' are what people type when they search; 'oftenWith' and 'neededBy' name other commands in this file. Expanded with system, hardware, network, sound, display, security and development tools.

commands.name: ls
commands.what: Lists what is in a folder: its files and folders.

examples.meaning: what is in the folder you are in
everything in your home folder, hidden files too, with sizes, owners and dates
the package cache, with sizes people can read (K, M, G)

options.meaning: long list: permissions, owner, size, date
all: also hidden files (names starting with a dot)
with -l: sizes as K, M, G instead of bytes
recursive: the folders inside, and theirs

commands.name: cd
commands.what: Changes the folder you are in (the working directory). It is part of the shell itself, not a program.

examples.meaning: go into your Downloads folder
go up one folder
go back to the folder you were in before
go home (~)

commands.name: pwd
commands.what: Prints the folder you are in (print working directory).

examples.meaning: for example /home/you/Downloads

commands.name: mkdir
commands.what: Makes a new folder (make directory).

examples.meaning: a folder named Projects, inside the folder you are in
the whole path at once, making each missing folder on the way
a folder only you can open (see chmod for the numbers)

options.meaning: parents: make the folders on the way too; no error if it already exists
mode: its permissions at once, like chmod (e.g. -m 700)

commands.name: rmdir
commands.what: Removes a folder, only if it is empty — the safe way to remove a folder.

examples.meaning: removes it if it is empty; refuses otherwise

options.meaning: also the parent folders, if they become empty

commands.name: touch
commands.what: Makes an empty file, or sets an existing file's date to now.

examples.meaning: an empty notes.txt (an existing one is left as it is, only its date changes)

commands.name: cp
commands.what: Copies files and folders.

examples.meaning: a copy beside it
a whole folder onto a USB stick
a folder exactly as it is: permissions, dates and links kept

options.meaning: recursive: folders and everything in them
archive: like -r, and keeps permissions, owners, dates and links
interactive: ask before replacing a file

commands.caution: cp replaces a file of the same name without asking, unless you add -i.

commands.name: mv
commands.what: Moves files and folders, or renames them.

examples.meaning: renames draft.txt
moves every .png here into Pictures

options.meaning: interactive: ask before replacing a file

commands.caution: mv replaces a file of the same name without asking, unless you add -i.

commands.name: rm
commands.what: Removes files (and, with -r, folders). There is no rubbish bin: what rm removes is gone.

examples.meaning: removes one file
a folder and everything in it, asking for each file

options.meaning: recursive: folders and everything in them
force: never ask, no error for missing files — careful

commands.caution: No undo. Read the command twice; sudo rm -rf can erase the whole system.

commands.name: ln
commands.what: Makes a link: a second name that points at a file or folder.

examples.meaning: ~/.zshrc becomes a pointer to the file in ~/dotfiles

options.meaning: symbolic link (the usual kind, works across disks and for folders)
replace a link that is already there

commands.name: cat
commands.what: Prints a file's text into the terminal (or joins several files).

examples.meaning: which distribution this is
two files joined into a third

commands.name: less
commands.what: Shows a long text one screen at a time. Space or Page Down goes on, b goes back, / searches, q quits.

examples.meaning: read pacman's settings
any long output, a screen at a time

commands.name: head
commands.what: Shows the first lines of a file or of an output (10 unless told).

examples.meaning: its first 20 lines

commands.name: tail
commands.what: Shows the last lines of a file (10 unless told); with -f, keeps showing new lines as they are written.

examples.meaning: pacman's last 50 actions
watch it live (Ctrl+C stops)

commands.name: nano
commands.what: A simple text editor in the terminal. Its keys are shown at the bottom: ^ means Ctrl. Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X quits.

examples.meaning: edit your shell's settings
edit a system file (system files need sudo)

commands.name: vim
commands.what: A powerful text editor with modes: i to type, Esc to stop typing, :w to save, :q to quit (:q! quits without saving).

examples.meaning: edit notes.txt

commands.name: find
commands.what: Finds files and folders by name, size, date or type, walking through every folder inside the one you give.

examples.meaning: every PDF in your home
files over 500 MB in Downloads
settings files a package update left waiting

options.meaning: f for files, d for folders
by age in days: -7 is changed this week
remove what it finds — check without it first

commands.name: grep
commands.what: Finds lines of text that contain a word or pattern — in files, or in another command's output.

examples.meaning: lines with error, any case
installed packages with python in their name
which file under /etc sets it, with line numbers

options.meaning: recursive: every file in a folder

commands.name: which
commands.what: Says where a command's program is, or nothing if there is none.

examples.meaning: for example /usr/bin/python

commands.name: file
commands.what: Says what kind of file something is, by looking inside it (not by its name).

examples.meaning: for example: a PNG image, or a gzip archive

commands.name: sort
commands.what: Sorts lines: alphabetically, or by number.

examples.meaning: your home's folders from smallest to largest

commands.name: uniq
commands.what: Drops lines that repeat the line just before (so sort first); with -c, counts them.

examples.meaning: each name with how often it appears, most first

commands.name: wc
commands.what: Counts lines, words and characters.

examples.meaning: how many packages you installed yourself

commands.name: diff
commands.what: Shows how two files differ, line by line.

examples.meaning: your settings against the new default a package update left

options.meaning: unified: the easiest way to read changes (- removed, + added)

commands.name: echo
commands.what: Prints the words you give it. Used to show messages, or to write a line into a file.

examples.meaning: your home folder's path

commands.name: tee
commands.what: Writes what it receives into a file and shows it too. With sudo, the usual way to write into a system file from a command.

examples.meaning: writes a line into a system file (sudo echo > file would not work: the > is not run as root)

options.meaning: append: add to the end instead of replacing

commands.name: sed
commands.what: Changes text as it passes through: most often, replaces one word with another.

examples.meaning: shows notes.txt with every foo as bar (the file is not changed)
changes the file itself

options.meaning: in place: change the file itself

commands.name: awk
commands.what: Reads text in columns: picks out, adds up or rearranges the parts of each line.

examples.meaning: each disk with how full it is

options.meaning: what separates the columns (a space unless told)

commands.name: xargs
commands.what: Turns lines it receives into the arguments of another command.

examples.meaning: removes every .tmp file found here

options.meaning: run nothing when it receives nothing

commands.name: chmod
commands.what: Changes who may read, write and open (run) a file or folder. The numbers: each digit is owner, group, everyone else; 4 read + 2 write + 1 run. 700 = only you, everything. 755 = you everything, others read and run. 644 = you read and write, others read. 600 = only you, read and write.

examples.meaning: lets it be run as a program
a private key only you can read (ssh refuses keys others can read)
a folder others may open and read, everything inside too

commands.name: chown
commands.what: Changes who owns a file or folder (needs sudo for files that are not yours).

examples.meaning: makes everything in Projects yours again

commands.name: sudo
commands.what: Runs one command as root (the system's own all-powerful user), after asking for your password. On Arch your user can use it when it is in the wheel group.

examples.meaning: updating the system needs root
a root shell, until you type exit — careful
forget the password now: the next sudo asks again

options.meaning: as another user instead of root (-u name)
list what you may run with sudo
ask for the password with a window (SUDO_ASKPASS) — how TuxCopilot asks
never ask: fail instead of asking for a password
refresh the remembered password without running anything
set HOME to the target user's home

commands.caution: Everything after sudo runs with full power over the system. Never sudo yay or makepkg: they refuse it, rightly.

commands.name: su
commands.what: Switches to another user (root, unless told) in this terminal, with that user's password.

examples.meaning: become otheruser, with their own settings

options.meaning: a login shell: the user's own environment

commands.name: whoami
commands.what: Prints the name of the user you are.

examples.meaning: your user name (root inside sudo)

commands.name: id
commands.what: Prints your user and the groups you are in (wheel lets you use sudo, docker lets you use Docker…).

examples.meaning: your user number and groups

commands.name: groups
commands.what: Prints the groups a user is in.

examples.meaning: your groups

commands.name: usermod
commands.what: Changes a user account — most often, adds you to a group. It takes effect after you log out and in again.

examples.meaning: lets you use Docker without sudo (log out and in)

options.meaning: append to these groups — without -a, you are removed from all others

commands.caution: Always -aG together: -G alone takes you out of every group not named, wheel too.

commands.name: passwd
commands.what: Changes a password: yours, or (with sudo) another user's.

examples.meaning: change your own password

commands.name: tar
commands.what: Packs folders into one archive file (.tar, .tar.gz, .tar.zst) and unpacks them.

examples.meaning: unpacks it here (any kind of .tar.*)
packs Documents, compressed by the name's ending
lists what is inside without unpacking

options.meaning: the archive file's name comes next
choose the compression from the name (.gz, .xz, .zst)
verbose: each file as it goes

commands.name: unzip
commands.what: Unpacks a .zip file.

examples.meaning: unpacks into a folder of its own

commands.name: zip
commands.what: Packs files into a .zip archive (the kind every computer opens).

examples.meaning: a folder as photos.zip

options.meaning: recursive: folders and everything in them

commands.name: curl
commands.what: Fetches something from a web address: shows it, or saves it.

examples.meaning: downloads a file under its own name
asks the Tor Project whether you come through Tor

options.meaning: save under the file's own name

commands.caution: Never pipe a download straight into bash (curl … | bash) from a site you don't trust: read it first.

commands.name: wget
commands.what: Downloads files from the web, carrying on if the connection breaks.

examples.meaning: downloads, picking up where a broken download stopped

commands.name: ping
commands.what: Checks whether another computer answers over the network, and how fast. Ctrl+C stops it.

examples.meaning: three tries: is the internet there, and does name lookup work?

commands.name: ip
commands.what: Shows (and sets) your network: addresses, interfaces, routes.

examples.meaning: each network interface with its address, one per line
where traffic goes (the default route is your router)

commands.name: ss
commands.what: Shows network connections and which programs listen on which ports.

examples.meaning: every port open for listening, with its program (sudo shows all programs)

commands.name: nmcli
commands.what: NetworkManager from the terminal: Wi-Fi, connections, devices.

examples.meaning: the Wi-Fi networks around
joins one, asking for its password

commands.name: ssh
commands.what: Opens a terminal on another computer, encrypted.

examples.meaning: logs in to that computer

commands.name: scp
commands.what: Copies files to or from another computer over ssh.

examples.meaning: into your home folder over there

commands.name: rsync
commands.what: Copies folders efficiently: only what changed. For backups and big copies, here or to another computer.

examples.meaning: copies Pictures, only what changed since last time

options.meaning: archive: everything kept as it is
also remove what is gone from the source — careful

commands.caution: A slash at the end of the source matters: dir/ copies what is inside, dir copies the folder itself.

commands.name: df
commands.what: Shows how full each disk is.

examples.meaning: every disk with its size, used and free space in G and M

commands.name: du
commands.what: Shows how much space folders and files take.

examples.meaning: your home's folders, smallest to largest

commands.name: free
commands.what: Shows memory: used, free, and available (what programs can still get).

examples.meaning: memory and swap in G and M

commands.name: lsblk
commands.what: Lists disks and their partitions, with where each is mounted.

examples.meaning: with each partition's filesystem and label

commands.name: mount
commands.what: Attaches a disk's filesystem at a folder, so its files appear there. Without arguments, lists what is mounted.

examples.meaning: the USB stick's first partition, at /mnt

commands.name: umount
commands.what: Detaches a mounted disk (do it before pulling a USB stick out).

examples.meaning: safe to unplug once it returns

commands.name: ps
commands.what: Lists running programs (processes) with their numbers (PIDs).

examples.meaning: Firefox's processes and their numbers

options.meaning: every process of every user, with details

commands.name: top
commands.what: Shows running programs live, the busiest first. q quits.

examples.meaning: what is using the computer right now

commands.name: kill
commands.what: Sends a signal to a program by its number: asks it to stop (the default), or forces it (-9).

examples.meaning: asks process 1234 to stop
forces it, when it does not answer

options.meaning: SIGKILL: stop at once, no cleanup

commands.name: pkill
commands.what: Stops programs by name instead of by number.

examples.meaning: asks every Firefox process to stop

commands.name: killall
commands.what: Stops every program with exactly this name.

examples.meaning: stops KDE's desktop shell (start it again with plasmashell &)

commands.name: uname
commands.what: Prints the kernel's name and version.

examples.meaning: the running kernel's version

commands.name: uptime
commands.what: How long the computer has been on, and how busy it has been.

examples.meaning: for example: up 2 days, 3 hours

commands.name: dmesg
commands.what: The kernel's own messages: hardware found, drivers, errors.

examples.meaning: only errors and warnings, readable

commands.name: lspci
commands.what: Lists the hardware inside: graphics card, network card, controllers.

examples.meaning: your graphics card and the driver it uses

commands.name: lsusb
commands.what: Lists what is plugged into USB.

examples.meaning: each USB device with its maker and model

commands.name: timedatectl
commands.what: Shows and sets the clock, the time zone, and time sync from the internet.

examples.meaning: the time, time zone, and whether it syncs
keep the clock right from the internet

commands.name: reboot
commands.what: Restarts the computer.

examples.meaning: after a kernel update, so the new one runs

commands.name: poweroff
commands.what: Shuts the computer down.

examples.meaning: turns it off

commands.name: man
commands.what: Opens a command's manual: everything it can do. Space goes on, / searches, q quits.

examples.meaning: pacman's whole manual

options.meaning: search every manual's title for a word

commands.name: pacman
commands.what: Arch's package manager: installs, updates and removes software from the official repositories.

examples.meaning: update everything
install Firefox
remove it, with what only it needed

commands.name: yay
commands.what: An AUR helper: installs packages from the AUR (made by people, not checked by Arch) as well as from the repositories. Run it without sudo.

examples.meaning: update everything, AUR packages too
install from the AUR (read its build script when asked)

commands.caution: AUR packages are made by people, not checked by Arch: read the build script yay shows.

commands.name: makepkg
commands.what: Builds a package from a PKGBUILD (the recipe in an AUR folder). Never with sudo.

examples.meaning: builds the package here, installs it and its dependencies

options.meaning: clean up the build files afterwards

commands.name: paccache
commands.what: Cleans pacman's cache of downloaded packages, keeping a few versions to go back to.

examples.meaning: keep the two newest versions of each package
remove every cached version of packages no longer installed

options.meaning: dry run: show what would go

commands.name: pacdiff
commands.what: Finds the .pacnew files updates left beside your settings files, and helps merge them: view, merge, keep or remove each.

examples.meaning: goes through each waiting .pacnew with you

commands.name: reflector
commands.what: Picks fast, up-to-date Arch mirrors (the servers packages come from) and writes them into pacman's mirror list.

examples.meaning: the 10 most recent mirrors, fastest first

options.meaning: only the N most recently synced

commands.name: mkinitcpio
commands.what: Builds the initramfs: the small image the kernel starts from, before your disks are opened.

examples.meaning: rebuild it for every installed kernel (after changing /etc/mkinitcpio.conf)

commands.name: flatpak
commands.what: Installs and runs Flatpak apps (from Flathub), each in its own sandbox.

examples.meaning: install Krita from Flathub
update every Flatpak app
remove runtimes no app uses

commands.name: systemctl
commands.what: Controls services (programs systemd runs in the background): start, stop, switch on at boot, see their state.

examples.meaning: is it running, with its last log lines
start it now and at every boot
what failed

commands.name: journalctl
commands.what: Reads the system's log: what services, the kernel and programs wrote.

examples.meaning: only errors since this boot
one service's log, live

commands.name: git
commands.what: Keeps the history of a project's files, and downloads (clones) projects from GitHub, GitLab and the AUR.

examples.meaning: downloads an AUR package's folder
brings a clone up to date

commands.name: firewall-cmd
commands.what: Controls firewalld, the firewall: which services and ports may be reached from the network.

examples.meaning: what the active zone lets in
closes SSH, for good

commands.name: nft
commands.what: The kernel's own firewall rules, written directly (firewalld writes them for you).

examples.meaning: every rule there is now

commands.name: snapper
commands.what: Takes and lists snapshots of a Btrfs filesystem: the state of your system at a moment, to go back to.

examples.meaning: the snapshots of / (snap-pac takes one before and after each pacman run)
one now, with a note

commands.name: docker
commands.what: Runs apps in containers: each with what it needs, apart from the system.

examples.meaning: the containers running
starts the app described in compose.yaml here

commands.name: ollama
commands.what: Runs AI language models on your own computer.

examples.meaning: downloads a model
chats with it in the terminal

commands.name: torsocks
commands.what: Sends one terminal program's connections through the Tor service.

examples.meaning: IsTor:true means it went through Tor

commands.name: stat
commands.what: Shows a file's metadata: size, permissions, owner, dates, file type — in one block.

examples.meaning: size, blocks, permissions, owner, dates, file type
name, size in bytes, last modified — in a custom format

options.meaning: format: a custom string (%n name, %s size, %y mtime, %F type, %U owner, %G group)
filesystem status (free/total blocks, type) instead of a file
follow a symlink: stat what it points at

commands.name: dd
commands.what: Copies raw bytes between files and devices — the classic way to write an ISO to a USB stick.

examples.command: sudo dd if=archlinux.iso of=/dev/sdb bs=4M status=progress
examples.meaning: writes the Arch installer ISO to a USB stick (the whole device, not a partition)
a 100 MB file of zeros

options.meaning: block size: how many bytes to read/write at a time (e.g. 4M)
conversions: noerror (continue on read errors), sync (pad), notrunc (don't truncate output)

commands.caution: dd writes raw bytes — point of= at the wrong device and you erase it. Check lsblk twice first.

commands.name: fsck
commands.what: Checks and repairs a filesystem for errors — run when a partition won't mount or after a crash. Only on a filesystem that is NOT mounted (a USB stick you unplugged from the file manager, or from a live USB): repairing a mounted one can wreck it. On btrfs (CachyOS's default) fsck does nothing — btrfs check is its checker.

examples.meaning: checks the USB stick's first partition (unmount it first)
only looks: reports problems on the (unmounted) USB stick and changes nothing

options.meaning: automatically repair (don't ask) (for ext4: fsck passes it on to e2fsck)
answer yes to every repair question (for ext4: fsck passes it on to e2fsck)
answer no: check only, change nothing (for ext4: fsck passes it on to e2fsck)
force a check even if the filesystem looks clean (for ext4: fsck passes it on to e2fsck)
scan for bad blocks (slow) (for ext4: fsck passes it on to e2fsck)

commands.caution: Unmount the filesystem before checking it. fsck on a mounted filesystem can corrupt it.

commands.name: smartctl
commands.what: Reads SMART health data from a disk — early-warning signs of failure, temperature, run hours.

examples.meaning: everything SMART knows about the first disk
just the pass/fail health verdict

options.meaning: all: every SMART attribute and log
attributes: the table of values (raw, normalised, worst, threshold)
run a test: short, long, offline
device type: ata, scsi, nvme (auto-detected usually)

commands.name: lscpu
commands.what: Prints the CPU's architecture: model, cores, threads, cache, flags, virtualisation features.

examples.meaning: the CPU's model, core count, cache size, and feature flags
one line per CPU (core, socket, die, cache) — good for scripts

options.meaning: extended: one line per logical CPU
parsable: a single line of comma-separated values

commands.name: lsmod
commands.what: Lists the kernel modules currently loaded (drivers, filesystems, crypto).

examples.meaning: the first ten loaded modules
is a video driver module loaded?

commands.name: modprobe
commands.what: Loads or unloads a kernel module (driver) by name.

examples.meaning: loads the Intel HDA sound driver
unloads the webcam driver

options.meaning: dry run: say what it would do, change nothing
show the whole module configuration (every alias, option and blacklist)

commands.name: sensors
commands.what: Reads temperature, fan and voltage sensors from the motherboard and CPU.

examples.meaning: every sensor reading — CPU temp, fan RPM, voltages
JSON output, for scripts and dashboards

options.meaning: unknown: show raw readings for unsupported chips

commands.caution: First time? Run sudo sensors-detect once so it learns which chips you have.

commands.name: coredumpctl
commands.what: Lists and inspects core dumps — what crashed, when, and what to feed a debugger.

examples.meaning: every crash the system recorded, newest last
details of the most recent crash
start gdb on the most recent core dump

options.meaning: show detailed info about a coredump
print the core to stdout (pipe to a file)
open a debugger (gdb) on the coredump
operate only on the most recent coredump

commands.name: systemd-analyze
commands.what: Profiles systemd: boot time, the time-critical chain, unit security, calendar expressions.

examples.meaning: how long the boot took (firmware + loader + kernel + userspace)
every unit sorted by how long it took to start
the tree of units that gated boot

options.meaning: SVG of the whole boot timeline — write to a file

commands.name: acpi
commands.what: Shows battery, AC adapter, thermal and fan state from the kernel.

examples.meaning: battery percentage and charge/discharge state
everything: battery, thermal, fan, AC adapter

options.meaning: details: capacity, cycle count, design capacity

commands.name: upower
commands.what: Queries UPower for battery and power device details (the daemon behind acpi's data).

examples.meaning: dump every power device's full state
object paths of every power device

options.meaning: just the battery's details: charge, health, time left
list object paths of every device
show one device, by the object path --enumerate lists

commands.name: pactl
commands.what: Controls PipeWire-Pulse / PulseAudio from the terminal: sinks, sources, volumes, defaults.

examples.meaning: audio outputs (speakers, headphones), one per line
set the default output's volume to 80%
make this output the default

commands.name: xrandr
commands.what: Shows and sets displays under X11: resolution, refresh rate, position, mirroring.

examples.meaning: every display and the resolutions it supports
set HDMI to 1080p, to the right of the laptop screen
dim the laptop screen to 70%

options.meaning: place this display to the right of another
place this display to the left of another
enable at preferred settings if connected

commands.caution: xrandr is X11 only. On Wayland, use wlr-randr, kscreen-doctor, or your compositor's settings.

commands.name: fc-list
commands.what: Lists installed fonts by family, and finds which font matches a pattern.

examples.meaning: the first ten installed fonts
just family names (deduped)
only monospace fonts

options.meaning: verbose: full font pattern (file, family, style, lang, spacing)

commands.name: dig
commands.what: Queries DNS directly: resolves a name to its address, or follows the chain from the root.

examples.meaning: the A records (IPv4) for archlinux.org
just the IP, nothing else
mail exchangers for the domain
reverse lookup: which name points at this IP

options.meaning: only the answer, one per line
follow the delegation chain from the root servers down
reverse lookup of an IP address
query type: A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, CNAME, ANY…

commands.name: nmap
commands.what: Scans a host or network for open ports, running services, and the OS behind them.

ping sweep: which hosts are up on this network

version detection: probe the service behind each open port
ping scan: just check which hosts are up, no ports
ports to scan (e.g. -p 22,80,443 or -p- for all 65535)
aggressive: OS + version + script + traceroute in one

commands.name: bluetoothctl
commands.what: Controls Bluetooth from the terminal: scan, pair, connect, trust, remove devices.

examples.meaning: start scanning for discoverable devices (Ctrl+D to exit)
pair with a device by its MAC address
connect to a paired device
list every paired device

commands.name: rfkill
commands.what: Shows and toggles the hardware radio kill switch — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, WWAN, WIMAX.

examples.meaning: every radio device and whether it is soft/hard blocked

options.meaning: list devices and their block state
soft-block a device (wifi, bluetooth, all, or index)
unblock a soft-blocked device (can't undo a hardware switch)

commands.name: grub-mkconfig
commands.what: Regenerates GRUB's config (grub.cfg) from /etc/default/grub and the scripts in /etc/grub.d.

examples.meaning: rebuild the boot menu after editing /etc/default/grub

options.meaning: output: where to write the generated grub.cfg

commands.what: Shows and edits the UEFI boot menu: entries, order, timeout, BootNext.

examples.meaning: current boot order and every entry
create a new boot entry

commands.name: fwupdmgr
commands.what: Checks and installs firmware updates for the BIOS, dock, SSD, and other LVFS-supported devices.

examples.meaning: every device fwupd can update
available firmware updates
apply all pending firmware updates

commands.name: gpg
commands.what: Signs, verifies, encrypts and decrypts with PGP keys — and manages your keyring.

examples.meaning: public keys in your keyring
verify a detached signature against a file

push a key to a keyserver

commands.what: Creates, inspects and manages SSH key pairs — for passwordless logins and Git over SSH.

examples.meaning: generate an Ed25519 key (recommended) with a comment

commands.name: tmux
commands.what: A terminal multiplexer: sessions that survive a disconnect, windows and panes inside them.

examples.meaning: start a named session 'work'
list running sessions
reattach to the 'work' session

options.meaning: create a new session (-s for a name)

commands.caution: Inside tmux, the prefix is Ctrl+B then a key. Detach with Ctrl+B D, not exit.
